Review the claims of need C005-CH1.

Claims:
1. The KL-Patch 72 device consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is active, limiting battery life to barely the full 72-hour wear period in active patients; researchers must find a way to cut active current draw by at least 35% while maintaining ECG sampling rate at 250 Hz or above (C005-CH1). 5. Lab equipped for electronics prototyping, signal acquisition testing, and device-level EMC pre-compliance testing. [C005]
6. ECG sampling rate cannot drop below 250 Hz or the clinical validity of the signal is affected. [C005-CH1]
7. The device runs FreeRTOS on an ARM Cortex-M4 with a Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 for BLE communication. [C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware Engineer — Low-Power BLE Systems]
8. The battery capacity is 54 mAh lithium cell. [C005-CH1]

Review the claims of need C001-CH1.
It is about: company ArmaturaSec d.o.o. (C001), challenge C001-CH1.

Claims:
1. ArmaturaSec has collected several terabytes of normal Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP traffic captures from client sites over three years, but no confirmed malicious traffic examples exist (C001-CH1). 6. Method must be explainable in plain language to plant managers [C001-CH1]
7. Inference must run on-device without affecting packet forwarding latency [C001-CH1]
8. One to two engineers available part-time with access to traffic archives, hardware bench, and firmware codebase under NDA [C001]

[C005-CH1] challenge · Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz. · company C005
Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.

The KL-Patch 72 runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell. At rest, current draw is manageable, but the moment Bluetooth is advertising or streaming, we see peaks that push daily consumption to 18 mAh. For an average patient that leaves about 18 mAh in reserve across three days, which is fine. The problem is active patients — people who trigger more frequent data syncs because they are moving and the device is flagging events. In a cardiology population that is not a small group. We have already tuned BLE advertising intervals and moved to BLE 5.0 long-range PHY for some use cases, and we switched to a lower-power MCU variant last year. We are now within a few milliamps of what we think we can achieve through firmware changes alone. We need someone who understands the full power budget — radio duty cycling, ADC configuration, memory access patterns — and can find where the remaining headroom is. The constraint is hard: sampling rate cannot drop below 250 Hz or the clinical validity of the signal is affected. We have instrumented referen…[+2124 chars]

Our appliance firmware update process currently requires a technician on-site at the customer's substation; we want secure over-the-air updates, but every approach we've prototyped either has an unacceptable attack surface or fails when the GPRS link drops mid-transfer.

Every time we release a firmware update we have to send someone to the customer site to plug in a USB drive. For a substation forty kilometres outside Novi Sad that is manageable. For a client in a mountain valley in Bosnia it means a full day of travel. We want to push updates over the cellular link the appliance already uses for remote monitoring. We have prototyped three approaches. The first used a plain HTTPS pull with a signature check; a security review inside the team found the key storage on the current hardware was not good enough and an attacker with physical access could extract the signing key. The second used a dual-partition scheme with rollback; it worked fine on a stable connection but when the GPRS link dropped mid-transfer the bootloader left the device in a state we could not recover remotely, which is unacceptable at an unmanned site. The third prototype added a download manager with resume support but the code size pushed us over the flash budget on our older hardware variant. Three clients in Serbia and one in Bosnia asked us to provide a risk quantification report in euros — how much financial loss a specific vulnerability exposes them to — and we have no methodology for that; it's becoming a dealbreaker in contract negotiations.

Four clients — three in Serbia and one in Bosnia — have asked us to attach a euro figure to each finding in our SecAudit reports. They want to be able to tell their board: this vulnerability could cost us this much. We understand why they ask. They need to justify remediation budgets. The problem is we have never done this and we are not sure our current data supports it. We have records of what the vulnerabilities were, we know roughly what downtime costs for a water utility or an electricity distributor, and we can find published incident cost studies from Western Europe. What we do not have is a repeatable calculation method that holds up when a procurement officer asks how we arrived at the number. When we crossed two million documents in our Elasticsearch cluster last autumn, average search response time climbed from 0.4 seconds to 3.1 seconds. Our two database engineers have tried index sharding, query caching and hardware upgrades, and we got the time down to 2.4 seconds, but that is still unacceptable for a tool lawyers use dozens of times a day during trial preparation. The problem is that our index was designed for a corpus of a few hundred thousand documents and has not been fundamentally rethought since. We are adding roughly 15,000 new documents per month across three jurisdictions, so the situation will keep getting worse. Sources:
[C007/blog/2024-05-30/What We Learned at BioenergyEurope Showcase 2024 in Vienna] page · What We Learned at BioenergyEurope Showcase 2024 in Vienna · 2024 · company C007
Four of us from Suncokret Eko attended the BioenergyEurope Showcase in Vienna at the beginning of May. It was the first time we had taken a stand at an international trade event rather than just walking the floor, and it was worth the effort. The conversations that were most useful were not with the large equipment suppliers or the established pellet producers. They were with two groups of buyers we had not had direct contact with before. The first were German agricultural input distributors who are looking for biochar they can blend into soil conditioner products. Three of them asked about our production capacity and our quality documentation. Two of those three specifically asked about European Biochar Certificate registration, which confirmed for us that this certification is becoming a practical requirement for that market, not just a nice-to-have. The second group was buyers from the Netherlands running commercial greenhouse operations. They are interested in biochar as a growing medium component. Their fixed-carbon requirements were similar to the German buyers, and one of them was willing to discuss a pilot purchase even before full certification, on the condition that we could provide detailed lab analysis and a signed declaration of production method. Our pellet press breaks down about once a month because the sunflower husk feedstock has inconsistent moisture and particle size coming from different suppliers; downtime costs us roughly 15,000 EUR per incident when we have delivery commitments.

Our pellet press line goes down roughly once a month. The root cause is almost always the same: sunflower husk material arriving with moisture content or particle size outside the range the press can handle. When moisture is above 14% the dies clog; when there is too much fine dust mixed with coarser pieces the compression is uneven and we get bearing failures. Different suppliers deliver material that can vary from 8% to 22% moisture and from fine powder to chunks over 15 mm in the same delivery. Our current process is to check a sample at intake and reject loads that look bad, but our in-line NIR sensor only covers moisture and is not reliable below 10% or above 18%, and we have no automated particle-size check at all. Each breakdown costs us around 15,000 EUR in lost production, emergency maintenance and contract penalties. We have looked at pre-conditioning equipment, specifically a secondary hammer mill and a conditioning mixer, but we have not been able to confirm whether the spec we are considering would actually stabilise output enough to prevent failures. It is about: company Kardiolink a.d. (C005), challenge C005-CH2.

Claims:
1. The current pipeline applies a lossless compression step before upload, and the best consistently achieved is 3:1 ratio. [C005-CH2]

Sources:
[C005-CH2] challenge · We generate roughly 2 TB of raw ECG signal per month from field devices; our current lossless compression gives us only 3:1 ratio and storage costs at our cloud provider have reached €7,400 per month, which is unsustainable at the patient volume we are projecting for next year. · company C005
We generate roughly 2 TB of raw ECG signal per month from field devices; our current lossless compression gives us only 3:1 ratio and storage costs at our cloud provider have reached €7,400 per month, which is unsustainable at the patient volume we are projecting for next year.

Each KL-Patch 72 device generates roughly 900 MB of raw 16-bit ECG samples over its wear period at 250 Hz across three channels. We are deploying around 2,200 devices per month and growing. Our current pipeline applies a lossless compression step before upload, and the best we consistently achieve is 3:1, which still leaves us pushing about 2 TB to cloud storage each month. At €7,400 per month that is already a significant operating cost, and if we hit our projected 4,000 devices per month by Q2 next year the bill more than doubles. We looked at moving to lossy compression but our regulatory submission is built around lossless, so changing that requires a new clinical validation study and amendments to the technical file — not something we can do quickly. We also explored cold storage tiering and that saves maybe 15%, not enough. What we actually need is a better lossless algorithm that understands the structure of ECG signals: the quasi-periodic nature, the baseline wander, the noise characteristics of a wearable electrode. Four of us from Suncokret Eko attended the BioenergyEurope Showcase in Vienna at the beginning of May. It was the first time we had taken a stand at an international trade event rather than just walking the floor, and it was worth the effort. The conversations that were most useful were not with the large equipment suppliers or the established pellet producers. They were with two groups of buyers we had not had direct contact with before. The first were German agricultural input distributors who are looking for biochar they can blend into soil conditioner products. Three of them asked about our production capacity and our quality documentation. Our pellet press line goes down roughly once a month. The root cause is almost always the same: sunflower husk material arriving with moisture content or particle size outside the range the press can handle. Authors: Milena Savić (outside co-author); Filip Mijatović (R0905); Christoph Brandner (outside co-author); Luca Ferretti (outside co-author).
Keywords: instrumentation amplifier; CCIA; 65 nm CMOS; biopotential; sub-volt supply; reconfigurable gain.
This paper presents a capacitively-coupled instrumentation amplifier (CCIA) fabricated in a 65 nm low-power CMOS process and intended to serve both ECG (gain 40 dB, bandwidth 0.5–150 Hz) and EEG (gain 52 dB, bandwidth 0.5–80 Hz) acquisition modes selectable at run time via a 1-bit digital input. Supply voltage is 0.6 V drawn from an energy-harvesting rail. Total quiescent current across both amplifier stages is 350 nA. Input-referred noise integrated over the ECG band is 0.41 µVrms, and over the EEG band is 0.37 µVrms. The mid-band CMRR measured 91 dB for ECG mode and 88 dB for EEG mode. She spent six months as a visiting researcher at the University of Ljubljana in 2017. Since 2019 she has held an Assistant Professor position in the Department of Computing and Control Engineering. Review the claims of pair C005-CH1:R0905.
It is about: researcher Filip Mijatović (R0905) and company Kardiolink a.d. (C005), challenge C005-CH1.

Claims:
1. The challenge identifies radio duty cycling and ADC configuration as the two unresolved contributors to the 18 mAh/day budget after firmware tuning has been exhausted. [C005-CH1]
2. Mijatović co-authored work on duty-cycled MAC scheduling with deadline-aware slot allocation for wireless sensor nodes, reducing radio duty cycle and extending node lifetime in multi-sensor scenarios. [SYN-PUB-09632]
3. Mijatović worked part-time as a hardware design consultant for a Novi Sad-based startup on Bluetooth-connected pulse oximetry accessories, contributing to analogue signal chain and firmware. [R0905]
4. Filip Mijatović and Kardiolink would jointly profile and redesign the radio duty-cycling schedule and ADC configuration of the KL-Patch 72 to cut active current draw by ≥35%, using the company's Keysight N6705C current profiles and Mijatović's duty-cycled MAC scheduling and mixed-signal front-end methods, while holding ECG sampling at ≥250 Hz. [C005-CH1, SYN-PUB-09632, SYN-PUB-09637, SYN-PUB-07802]
5. The duty-cycling work covers IEEE 802.15.4 MAC scheduling; the challenge platform is BLE on nRF52840, and the records do not cover BLE-specific connection-interval or connection-event power optimization. [SYN-PUB-09632, C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware Engineer — Low-Power BLE Systems]

Activity recognition from chest-worn accelerometers (2021, journal, Wearable Sensing Review).
Authors: Maja Popović (R0906); Ana Stevanović (outside co-author); Miloš Radović (outside co-author).
Accurate activity recognition from chest-worn inertial measurement units is a prerequisite for context-aware physiological monitoring, yet most published benchmarks rely on wrist or hip placements. This study investigates the suitability of a single chest-mounted accelerometer for recognizing twelve daily-life activities including rest, walking, jogging, stair ascent and descent, cycling, and six sedentary postures. Features extracted in the time and frequency domains from three-axis acceleration signals were used to train and compare a k-nearest neighbor classifier, a random forest, and a support vector machine with radial basis function kernel. Data were collected from 45 healthy adults across a structured protocol lasting approximately 90 minutes per participant. The random forest achieved the highest overall accuracy of 92.3% in leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. A confusion analysis revealed that the chest location provides particularly strong discrimination between static postures, outperforming wrist placement on that sub-task. The findings support the integration of chest-worn accelerometers into ECG patch monitors for simultaneous cardiac and activity monitoring without additional sensor hardware.

Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.

The KL-Patch 72 runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell. At rest, current draw is manageable, but the moment Bluetooth is advertising or streaming, we see peaks that push daily consumption to 18 mAh. For an average patient that leaves about 18 mAh in reserve across three days, which is fine. The problem is active patients — people who trigger more frequent data syncs because they are moving and the device is flagging events. In a cardiology population that is not a small group. Review the claims of pair C002-CH1:R0322.
It is about: researcher Emilija Zec (R0322) and company Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o. (C002), challenge C002-CH1.

Claims:
1. The company needs a method to flag students guessing rather than learning, evidenced by high platform scores but poor paper-test performance (C002-CH1). [C002-CH1]
2. Emilija Zec co-authored speed–accuracy response-time models and mixture models that separate engaged from disengaged responding in assessment contexts (SYN-PUB-03985, SYN-PUB-03988). [SYN-PUB-03985, SYN-PUB-03988]
3. Emilija Zec co-authored Bayesian knowledge-tracing variants and hidden Markov models for tracking learner cognitive states from interaction logs, with extensions to label-free estimation from unstructured logs (SYN-PUB-03632, SYN-PUB-03990, SYN-PUB-02526). [SYN-PUB-03632, SYN-PUB-03990, SYN-PUB-02526]
4. Emilija Zec led DIAGTRACE (SYN-PRJ-0076), a national research project that developed psychometric methods for inferring cognitive skill states from behavioural trace data in digital learning platforms. [SYN-PRJ-0076]
5. Emilija Zec co-authored alignment studies between platform-generated ability scores and summative grades across multiple subjects (SYN-PUB-03992), directly matching the company's observed score–test gap (C002-CH1). [SYN-PUB-03992, C002-CH1]
6. The clickstream logs include attempt count and time-on-question but no eye-tracking or free-text data; the records cover richer trace data in some studies (SYN-PUB-03991), so the method must be confirmed to work on the available CSV fields alone. [SYN-PUB-03991, C002-CH1]
7. The constraint that output must be explainable to teachers without statistical training (C002/job/2024-06-01) requires an additional interpretability layer beyond the psychometric models; the records do not describe prior work on non-technical teacher-facing interfaces. [C002/job/2024-06-01/Freelance Data Analyst — Learning Outcomes Project (Short-Term Contract)]

It is about: researcher Danilo Mitrović (R1006) and company Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o. (C002), challenge C002-CH1.

Claims:
1. The company needs a method to flag students guessing rather than learning from two school years of clickstream logs (C002-CH1). [C002-CH1]
2. Danilo Mitrović co-authored work on longitudinal modelling of learning management system clickstream sequences using latent variable models including hidden Markov models and latent profile analysis (SYN-PUB-10456, SYN-PUB-10459). [SYN-PUB-10456, SYN-PUB-10459]
3. Danilo Mitrović co-authored sequence clustering and temporal pattern analysis of engagement trajectories using dynamic time warping and k-medoids clustering on clickstream data (SYN-PUB-10455). [SYN-PUB-10455]
4. Danilo Mitrović completed a four-month consultancy with an e-learning content provider in Novi Sad, advising on learner progress scoring systems for a digital platform (R1006). [R1006]
5. Using the company's clickstream logs (C002-CH1), Danilo Mitrović would apply latent variable models and sequence clustering on the attempt-count and time-on-question trajectories (SYN-PUB-10456, SYN-PUB-10455, SYN-PUB-10459) to identify behavioural profiles consistent with random clicking, and would build a prediction model (SYN-PUB-10454, SYN-PUB-10457) that flags at-risk students in a form teachers can act on before the 2025–26 school year. Review the claims of pair C002-CH1:R0837.
It is about: researcher Vukica Arsić (R0837) and company Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o. (C002), challenge C002-CH1.

Claims:
1. The company needs to flag students who are guessing in a game-based learning platform used in primary schools (C002-CH1). [C002-CH1]
2. Vukica Arsić co-authored work on interaction-log analysis to predict post-test performance from tablet-logged session data (SYN-PUB-09075, SYN-PUB-09080). [SYN-PUB-09075, SYN-PUB-09080]
3. Vukica Arsić co-authored an embedded assessment framework for distinguishing performance indicators, inferential indicators, and post-game probes in educational games without disrupting gameplay (SYN-PUB-06923). [SYN-PUB-06923]
4. Using the company's clickstream logs (C002-CH1), Vukica Arsić would apply interaction-log analysis methods developed for predicting post-test performance from tablet session data (SYN-PUB-09075, SYN-PUB-09080) and the embedded assessment framework for distinguishing performance indicators from inferential indicators in game sessions (SYN-PUB-06923) to identify behavioural signals in the logs that separate genuine learning from random clicking. [C002-CH1, SYN-PUB-09075, SYN-PUB-09080, SYN-PUB-06923]
5. The records cover interaction-log analysis and prediction of outcomes but do not describe a method specifically for separating guessing from genuine responding in existing logs; the work focuses on game design and outcome evaluation rather than anomaly detection in response processes. [SYN-PUB-09075, SYN-PUB-09080, SYN-PUB-06923]
6. The company's constraint requires a testable output before the 2025–26 school year (C002-CH1); the researcher's prior work involves multi-school experimental trials (SYN-PRJ-0281) whose timelines may not fit a single-year analytical project. [C002-CH1, SYN-PRJ-0281]

Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.

The KL-Patch 72 runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell. At rest, current draw is manageable, but the moment Bluetooth is advertising or streaming, we see peaks that push daily consumption to 18 mAh. For an average patient that leaves about 18 mAh in reserve across three days, which is fine. The problem is active patients — people who trigger more frequent data syncs because they are moving and the device is flagging events. In a cardiology population that is not a small group. We have already tuned BLE advertising intervals and moved to BLE 5.0 long-range PHY for some use cases, and we switched to a lower-power MCU variant last year. Review the claims of profile R0057.
It is about: researcher Lazar Šarić (R0057).

Claims:
1. Inter-beat redundancy in cardiac signals using differential pulse-code modulation of DCT coefficients with arithmetic coding. [SYN-PUB-00757]
2. Real-time encoding latency suitable for medical device applications, achieving per-beat latency of 0.4 ms on a standard laptop CPU and computational complexity tractable for microcontroller deployment. [SYN-PUB-00755, SYN-PUB-00754]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-00757] publication · Exploiting Inter-Beat Redundancy in ECG Compression via Differential Pulse-Code Modulation of DCT Coefficients · 2018 · researchers R0057
Exploiting Inter-Beat Redundancy in ECG Compression via Differential Pulse-Code Modulation of DCT Coefficients (2018, journal, IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Coding and Compression).
Authors: Klaus Binder (outside co-author); Lazar Šarić (R0057); Dragan Petković (outside co-author).
Keywords: inter-beat redundancy; DPCM; DCT; arithmetic coding; atrial fibrillation.
Consecutive cardiac beats in sinus rhythm show high morphological similarity, so their DCT coefficient sequences are strongly correlated across time. This paper models each lead's DCT coefficient track as a first-order autoregressive process and applies differential pulse-code modulation (DPCM) along the beat index rather than within a single beat. A predictor is trained on the first 30 seconds of each record and updated every 60 seconds to track slow morphological drift. Arithmetic coding is applied to the residual with a Laplacian model for the dominant low-frequency coefficients and a Cauchy model for higher-frequency ones. On a corpus of 48 single-lead records at 500 Hz, mean PRD is 1.4% at a compression ratio of 12.7:1, compared to 9.3:1 for independent per-beat DCT coding at matched PRD. The improvement degrades gracefully to 10.1:1 in the presence of atrial fibrillation, where inter-beat morphology is less predictable.

Review the claims of profile R0641.
It is about: researcher Branislav Stojanović (R0641).

Claims:
1. ECG compression on wearable Cortex-M0 nodes using embedded wavelet lifting and BLE transmission. [SYN-PUB-03183]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-03183] publication · Embedded Wavelet Lifting for ECG Compression on Wearable Cortex-M0 Nodes · 2015 · researchers R0251, R0641
Embedded Wavelet Lifting for ECG Compression on Wearable Cortex-M0 Nodes (2015, journal, Biomedical Engineering: Applications, Basis and Communications).
Authors: Slobodan Dražić (outside co-author); Ivana Horvatić (outside co-author); Tibor Takács (R0251); Branislav Stojanović (R0641); Christoph Fiedler (outside co-author).
Keywords: ECG compression; wavelet lifting; wearable; Cortex-M0; BLE; PRD.
Electrocardiogram data transmitted from chest-patch wearables place a disproportionate load on BLE bandwidth. We ported a fixed-point integer lifting-scheme wavelet transform (5/3 Le Gall filter) to an ARM Cortex-M0 running at 48 MHz and paired it with a simple threshold quantiser and arithmetic coder. The implementation stores all intermediate coefficients in 12 kB of SRAM, fitting within the budget of low-cost microcontrollers. Compression was evaluated on 30-minute, two-lead recordings from 18 subjects sampled at 500 Hz. The scheme achieved a mean compression ratio of 9.4:1 at a percent root-mean-square difference (PRD) of 2.7%, which is within the clinically acceptable range for rhythm monitoring. QRS peak locations in reconstructed signals deviated by a mean of 1.2 ms from reference annotations. Runtime was 1.8 ms per 500-sample frame, leaving the processor idle for 64% of each sampling period. Power consumption during active compression was 3.1 mW.

Authors: Jelena Bosnić (outside co-author); Danilo Mitrović (R1006); Radovan Ilić (outside co-author); Zuzana Kmeťová (R0595).
Keywords: survival analysis; time-to-mastery; mixed-effects models; competency; mathematics education.
This paper frames competency attainment in undergraduate mathematics as a time-to-event outcome and applies mixed-effects parametric survival models to longitudinal assessment data. Records from 2,240 students completing a multi-module calculus sequence over five academic years were analysed. The outcome was defined as the week in which a student first demonstrated sustained mastery on adaptive quizzes, operationalised as three consecutive passing scores above 80 %. A log-logistic accelerated failure time model with random student and instructor intercepts provided the best fit (log-likelihood ratio test against Weibull, p < 0.001). Time-to-mastery was significantly shortened by higher prior achievement scores and by weekly formative quiz completion, and was lengthened by patterns of concentrated last-minute access. The paper contributes a reusable feature engineering pipeline for Moodle log data and provides worked R code as a supplementary appendix.

The KL-Patch 72 runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell. At rest, current draw is manageable, but the moment Bluetooth is advertising or streaming, we see peaks that push daily consumption to 18 mAh. How teachers in Serbian vocational schools design screencasts: a survey of practices and stated rationales (2020, journal, Pedagogy and Education in Serbia).
Authors: Dragan Subotić (outside co-author); Olivera Milanović (outside co-author); Sara Dobanovački (R0600); Boris Krstić (R0872); Vukica Arsić (R0837).
Keywords: teacher practices; screencast design; vocational schools; Vojvodina; multimedia learning principles.
Despite the growing use of teacher-produced screencasts in Serbian secondary vocational education, little is known about how teachers make design decisions. This study surveyed 214 vocational teachers across 37 schools in Vojvodina regarding their screencast production practices, tools used, awareness of multimedia learning principles, and self-reported rationales for design choices. Eighty-one per cent used default settings in their recording software without consulting instructional design guidelines. Awareness of the redundancy effect was low (14% correct identification on a scenario-based item). Teachers with prior ICT training were more likely to use segmentation and to limit on-screen text. Open-ended responses revealed that perceived student preference drove many decisions, including the widespread inclusion of full narration transcripts as captions. The findings indicate a gap between research-derived guidance and classroom practice, informing the design of teacher professional development programmes.

Review the claims of profile R0905.
It is about: researcher Filip Mijatović (R0905).

Claims:
1. Reconfigurable instrumentation amplifier for biopotential acquisition with selectable gain for ECG and EEG modes in 65 nm CMOS, and sub-threshold OTA-based ECG front-end in 180 nm CMOS. [SYN-PUB-09637, SYN-PUB-09629]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-09637] publication · A 0.6 V, 210 nW instrumentation amplifier with reconfigurable gain for multi-modal biopotential acquisition in 65 nm CMOS · 2026 · researchers R0905
A 0.6 V, 210 nW instrumentation amplifier with reconfigurable gain for multi-modal biopotential acquisition in 65 nm CMOS (2026, journal, IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I: Regular Papers).
Authors: Milena Savić (outside co-author); Filip Mijatović (R0905); Christoph Brandner (outside co-author); Luca Ferretti (outside co-author).
Keywords: instrumentation amplifier; CCIA; 65 nm CMOS; biopotential; sub-volt supply; reconfigurable gain.
This paper presents a capacitively-coupled instrumentation amplifier (CCIA) fabricated in a 65 nm low-power CMOS process and intended to serve both ECG (gain 40 dB, bandwidth 0.5–150 Hz) and EEG (gain 52 dB, bandwidth 0.5–80 Hz) acquisition modes selectable at run time via a 1-bit digital input. Supply voltage is 0.6 V drawn from an energy-harvesting rail. Total quiescent current across both amplifier stages is 350 nA. Input-referred noise integrated over the ECG band is 0.41 µVrms, and over the EEG band is 0.37 µVrms. The mid-band CMRR measured 91 dB for ECG mode and 88 dB for EEG mode. Electrode offset rejection was verified with offsets up to ±300 mV applied via a dc servo loop consuming 18 nA. The circuit was characterised on 20 dies; gain spread across dies was ±0.4 dB. Post-layout simulations and measured data are compared and show less than 6% discrepancy in noise and 3% in bandwidth.

Beat-Synchronous DCT Coding of Long-Term ECG Recordings (2015, conference, Proceedings of the International Symposium on Biomedical Engineering and Medical Informatics (SBEMI)).
Authors: Milena Vuković (outside co-author); Lazar Šarić (R0057); Ana Nikolić (outside co-author).
Keywords: Holter ECG; DCT; beat segmentation; compression ratio; PRD.
Long-term (Holter) ECG recordings present compression challenges because gradual heart-rate drift shifts beat boundaries relative to fixed analysis windows. This work proposes a beat-synchronous discrete cosine transform (DCT) coder in which each beat is individually segmented using a Pan-Tompkins R-peak detector, zero-padded or truncated to a uniform 512-sample frame, and transformed to the DCT domain. Coefficient quantisation thresholds are derived per lead from a short training segment of the same recording, adapting to inter-patient variability. Tested on 18 two-lead 24-hour recordings at 250 Hz sampled at the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina, the coder achieves a mean compression ratio of 9.3:1 at a percentage root-mean-square difference (PRD) of 1.8%, with diagnostic quality preserved as assessed by two cardiologists. The encoding latency per beat averages 0.4 ms on a standard laptop CPU, confirming real-time feasibility.

Cross-Course Generalisation of Clickstream-Based Performance Predictors: An Empirical Evaluation (2020, conference, Proceedings of the International Workshop on Educational Data Mining).
Authors: Danilo Mitrović (R1006); Stefan Vuković (outside co-author); Ivana Petrović (outside co-author); Marc Delacroix (outside co-author).
Keywords: transfer learning; cross-course prediction; random forest; LSTM; model evaluation.
Most clickstream-based prediction models are trained and tested within a single course, leaving their cross-course generalisability unclear. This paper reports a systematic evaluation in which six predictive models (logistic regression, random forest, gradient-boosted trees, an LSTM, a naive Bayes baseline, and a rules-based expert model) were trained on data from one course and evaluated on 11 other courses at the Faculty of Sciences. Data covered 3,100 unique students and 14 courses over three academic years. AUC values dropped by an average of 0.11 when models were applied without retraining to new courses, but transfer performance recovered to within 0.04 of in-course performance after fine-tuning on as few as 50 labelled instances from the target course. Feature importance was markedly inconsistent across courses, with quiz-attempt features being the most portable. The paper provides recommendations for practitioners deploying predictive analytics in heterogeneous institutional contexts.

Alignment between formative diagnostic inferences and summative grades: an IRT-based audit across six secondary-school subjects in Serbia (2024, journal, Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice).
Authors: Dragana Milošević (outside co-author); Katarina Vukić (outside co-author); Emilija Zec (R0322).
Keywords: formative assessment; summative grades; multidimensional IRT; grade inflation; secondary education.
Data from six secondary-school subjects—mathematics, Serbian language, biology, history, physics, and English—were collected from a digital learning management platform used by 3,412 students in 22 schools across Serbia during one academic year. For each subject, a multidimensional IRT model was estimated from platform quiz responses, and inferred diagnostic ability scores were compared to end-of-year teacher grades using Pearson and Spearman correlations, classification accuracy matrices, and Bland–Altman agreement plots. Correlations ranged from 0.51 (history) to 0.74 (mathematics). Systematic grade inflation relative to diagnostic scores was found in 14 of 22 schools, with a mean offset of 0.4 grade points on a five-point scale. Schools with higher diagnostic–grade alignment also showed lower within-school grade variance. The findings suggest that diagnostic platform scores and teacher grades measure partially overlapping but non-redundant constructs.

4. Fejsa co-authored work using eye-tracking analysis of student interaction with digital texts to inform accessible design (SYN-PUB-02649). [SYN-PUB-02649]
5. The published records cover accessible design and intervention evaluation broadly; no record specifically covers font readability trials for children with dyslexia as the primary research question. [SYN-PUB-02653, SYN-PUB-02651, SYN-PUB-02657]
6. The records cover digital learning environments and instructional materials; none document prior work in game-based or entertainment-software contexts, which may require methodological adaptation. [SYN-PUB-02652, SYN-PUB-02650, SYN-PRJ-0078]

Learning management systems accumulate course materials over years without systematic accessibility review. Colour-zone coding systems in hospital wayfinding: memorability and navigation efficiency in a multi-storey building simulation (2025, conference, Proceedings of the 15th European Symposium on Wayfinding Research, Ljubljana).
Authors: Ivana Zdravković (outside co-author); Annamária Szűcs (outside co-author); Đorđe Milovanović (outside co-author); Stefan Ostojić (R0041).
Keywords: colour-zone coding; wayfinding; multi-storey hospital; colour vision deficiency; redundant coding.
Colour-zone coding assigns a distinct colour to each functional zone or floor of a hospital, aiming to reduce cognitive load during navigation. This study tested whether participants could correctly associate six colour codes with their corresponding zones after a single briefing exposure, and whether this association aided navigation in a multi-storey virtual building simulation. Seventy-two participants were divided into a colour-coded sign condition and a text-only sign condition. In the virtual building, navigation to six targets was timed and error-counted over three consecutive trials. After three trials, colour-coded condition participants committed fewer wrong-floor errors (mean 0.8 vs. 2.1 per participant) and showed steeper learning curves. However, 18 participants reported colour vision deficiency or difficulty; post-hoc analysis showed their error rates were equivalent across conditions, indicating that colour coding without secondary coding (shape or pattern) provides no benefit for this group. Review the claims of pair C001-CH1:R1008.
It is about: researcher Krisztina Kiss (R1008) and company ArmaturaSec d.o.o. (C001), challenge C001-CH1.

Claims:
1. ArmaturaSec requires unsupervised anomaly detection trained only on normal traffic, with no confirmed malicious examples available and supervised classifiers already ruled out due to unacceptable false positive rates in real deployments. [C001-CH1, C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Trying to Use Public ICS Datasets for Anomaly Detection]
2. The researcher co-authored work on one-class SVM, Isolation Forest, autoencoders, and kernel density estimators for unsupervised anomaly detection in ICS traffic. [SYN-PUB-00492, SYN-PUB-10481, SYN-PUB-10480, SYN-PUB-10479, SYN-PUB-10478]
3. The researcher co-authored work on threshold calibration for ICS anomaly detectors using beta mixture models and unlabelled operational data to correct false positive rate miscalibration at deployment. [SYN-PUB-10480]
4. The researcher co-authored work on lightweight anomaly detection for embedded ICS gateways through weight quantisation and structured pruning of autoencoders, achieving millisecond-scale inference on ARM Cortex-A7 processors. [SYN-PUB-10239]
5. The researcher co-authored work on protocol-agnostic anomaly detection using byte-level features from ICS application payloads, demonstrated on Modbus, DNP3, and proprietary vendor protocols. [SYN-PUB-10483]
6. The on-device work (SYN-PUB-10239) covers ARM Cortex-A7 processors; whether the ProtoSense module uses the same processor class is not confirmed in the records. [SYN-PUB-10239, C001-CH1]
7. The published record covers Modbus and DNP3; BACnet/IP-specific baseline modelling is not evidenced in the researcher's work. [SYN-PUB-10483, C001-CH1]

Sources:
[C001-CH1] challenge · We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic a…[+13684 chars]

Review the claims of pair C001-CH1:R1015.
It is about: researcher Vuk Đukić (R1015) and company ArmaturaSec d.o.o. (C001), challenge C001-CH1.

Claims:
1. ArmaturaSec requires an unsupervised method that produces no false positives from normal-only training data, without relying on labelled attack examples. [C001-CH1, C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Trying to Use Public ICS Datasets for Anomaly Detection]
2. The researcher co-authored work on unsupervised anomaly detection on industrial control system protocols using autoencoder-based neural networks. [SYN-PUB-10523]
3. The researcher co-authored work on intrusion detection on resource-constrained IoT devices using compressed recurrent neural network models. [SYN-PUB-10531]
4. The researcher led the academic partner contribution to SECURE-ICS, an Innovation Fund project developing security monitoring for factory automation systems on Modbus, PROFINET, and EtherNet/IP protocols. [SYN-PRJ-0017]
5. The published record covers autoencoder-based detection on ICS protocols (SYN-PUB-10523) but does not evidence threshold calibration or sliding-window recalibration on unlabelled operational data specifically. [SYN-PUB-10523, C001-CH1]
6. The resource-constrained device work (SYN-PUB-10531) covers IoT devices using compressed RNNs; whether this extends to the ProtoSense module's specific hardware without affecting forwarding latency is not evidenced. [SYN-PUB-10531, C001]

Sources:

Review the claims of pair C001-CH1:R0416.
It is about: researcher Ksenija Hadžić (R0416) and company ArmaturaSec d.o.o. (C001), challenge C001-CH1.

Claims:
1. ArmaturaSec requires a method that learns normal behaviour from unlabelled captures only; automaton inference from normal traffic strings is an unsupervised, label-free approach. [C001-CH1]
2. The researcher co-authored work on anomaly detection in SCADA and protocol traffic by comparing observed message sequences against inferred finite automaton models. [SYN-PUB-04998]
3. The researcher co-authored work on passive inference of finite automata from labelled strings using state-merging algorithms, and developed GInferLib, an open-source Python library implementing seven grammatical inference algorithms. [SYN-PUB-04995, SYN-PUB-05000]
4. ArmaturaSec requires the method to be explainable in plain language to plant managers; finite automaton models of protocol behaviour can be presented as state diagrams that enumerate permitted message sequences. [C001-CH1]
5. The researcher's published anomaly detection work (SYN-PUB-04998) covers SCADA protocol traffic in general; Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP payload-level features are not specifically evidenced. [SYN-PUB-04998, C001-CH1]
6. No evidence in the researcher's record addresses on-device inference within the latency constraint required for the ProtoSense module. [C001, R0416]
7. Automaton inference methods may not capture continuous or numeric payload anomalies (e.g., register value drift in Modbus) as effectively as statistical or neural methods, covering primarily structural sequence deviations. [SYN-PUB-04998, C001-CH1]

Sources:

Log-Based Predictive Maintenance for Conveyor Belt Controllers: A Case Study from a Food-Processing Plant (2023, journal, Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence).
Authors: Vladana Vojnović (R0030); Milica Labus (outside co-author); Zoran Petrović (outside co-author).
Keywords: predictive maintenance; PLC logs; isolation forest; industrial IoT; Vojvodina.
Predictive maintenance using log data from industrial programmable logic controllers (PLCs) is explored in a food-processing facility in Vojvodina operating 14 conveyor belt lines. PLC diagnostic logs recording motor current deviations, sensor timeouts, and safety interlock triggers were collected over 18 months, yielding approximately 9.4 million log entries and 38 confirmed maintenance events. A combination of sliding-window frequency features and an isolation forest classifier trained on normal operating periods is used to flag degradation precursors. Leave-one-out cross-validation across the 38 events yields a mean warning lead time of 4.3 hours before failure with a precision of 0.79 and recall of 0.87. The paper describes practical challenges including irregular maintenance windows that contaminate normal-operation labels and proprietary log formats that required manual template construction.

Authors: Goran Radović (R0528); Milena Vukčević (outside co-author); Darko Petrović (outside co-author).
Keywords: Rusyn Cyrillic; parametric glyph design; skeleton model; UFO workflow; minority typeface.
Rusyn, a minority language officially recognised in Serbia and Croatia, uses a Cyrillic orthography that includes several characters absent from standard Serbian Cyrillic encodings. Existing digital fonts either omit these glyphs or render them through ad-hoc workarounds that break OpenType shaping. This paper proposes a parametric skeleton model for 14 Rusyn-specific glyphs, defining five interpolation axes—weight, contrast, x-height ratio, serif style, and counter aperture—using RoboFab-based Python scripting within a Unified Font Object (UFO) workflow. Skeleton nodes and handles are expressed as proportional functions of a master unit-per-em value, allowing consistent scaling across optical sizes. The model was validated by generating 48 instance fonts across axis combinations and subjecting them to readability assessments with 23 Rusyn-speaking participants recruited through the National Council of the Rusyn Minority in Novi Sad. Agreement scores measured on a five-point typographic naturalness scale reached a mean of 3.9 for serif instances and 3.6 for sans-serif instances, with the lowest scores associated with extreme contrast settings. We present GInferLib, an open-source Python library providing implementations of seven grammatical inference algorithms for deterministic and nondeterministic finite automata, including RPNI, EDSM, L*, NL*, and three recent state-merging variants. We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.

Our ProtoSense module watches Modbus and BACnet traffic and is supposed to flag anything that looks wrong. The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. A few of them have been running their networks for twenty years with no security monitoring at all, so if they were compromised they would not know. We have plenty of normal traffic — we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years — but we have nothing labelled as malicious. We tried building a supervised classifier once, fed it data from public ICS datasets, and it flagged so many false positives in real deployments that clients started switching the alerts off. [SYN-PRJ-0512] project · Federated Anomaly Detection Across Distributed Industrial Control System Sites · 2022 · researchers R1008
FEDICS: Federated Anomaly Detection Across Distributed Industrial Control System Sites (Interreg IPA Hungary–Serbia, 2022–2025).
Participants: R1008 coordinator.
Partners: Department of Automation and Applied Informatics, Budapest University of Technology; Faculty of Informatics, University of Debrecen; Vodovod Vojvodina d.o.o., Novi Sad (fictional regional water utility).
FEDICS developed federated learning protocols enabling anomaly detection models trained at geographically distributed ICS sites to be aggregated without exchanging raw network traffic. The project addressed privacy constraints common in critical infrastructure contexts and evaluated ensemble aggregation strategies for combining site-level one-class classifiers. Pilot deployments were conducted at two water utility control centres and two district heating substations across the Hungarian–Serbian border region. The project also produced a joint curriculum module on ICS cybersecurity delivered at partner universities. Key deliverables included open-source federated aggregation software, two datasets, and six joint publications by the consortium.

We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.

Our ProtoSense module watches Modbus and BACnet traffic and is supposed to flag anything that looks wrong. The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. A few of them have been running their networks for twenty years with no security monitoring at all, so if they were compromised they would not know. We have plenty of normal traffic — we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years — but we have nothing labelled as malicious. Keywords: IoT security; intrusion detection; recurrent neural networks; resource-constrained devices; anomaly detection.
Deploying intrusion detection directly on resource-constrained IoT devices such as microcontroller-based sensors and actuators presents fundamental challenges in terms of memory footprint, computational overhead, and energy consumption. This paper investigates the feasibility of implementing lightweight recurrent neural network models—specifically truncated LSTM and GRU variants—on devices with fewer than 256 KB of RAM. A model compression pipeline is developed that combines quantisation, pruning, and knowledge distillation to reduce model size by up to 94% relative to full-precision baselines, while preserving detection accuracy above 90% across standard IoT attack benchmarks. The compressed models are deployed on three representative IoT platforms and evaluated under realistic workload conditions. It is about: researcher Filip Mijatović (R0905) and company Kardiolink a.d. (C005), challenge C005-CH1.

Sources:
[C005-CH1] challenge · Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz. · company C005
Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.

The KL-Patch 72 runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell. At rest, current draw is manageable, but the moment Bluetooth is advertising or streaming, we see peaks that push daily consumption to 18 mAh. For an average patient that leaves about 18 mAh in reserve across three days, which is fine. The problem is active patients — people who trigger more frequent data syncs because they are moving and the device is flagging events. In a cardiology population that is not a small group. Claims:
1. ArmaturaSec's three failed update designs each broke on one of three constraints — key storage, mid-transfer recovery, or flash budget — that the challenge requires a single design to satisfy simultaneously (C001-CH2). [C001-CH2]
2. 4. Ana Rajić co-authored work on IEC 62443 industrial security standards compliance for OTA firmware update mechanisms, including mapping of security level requirements to cryptographic and transaction management techniques (SYN-PUB-03505). [SYN-PUB-03505]

Stack and Heap Memory Profiling of SPHINCS+ on RISC-V RV32IMC Without Hardware Multiplier (2021, journal, Journal of Cryptographic Engineering).
Authors: Miroslav Tešić (outside co-author); Milica Nikolić (R0503).
Keywords: SPHINCS+; hash-based signatures; RISC-V; memory profiling; stack optimisation.
SPHINCS+ is a stateless hash-based signature scheme selected for standardisation by NIST, but its relatively large signature sizes and tree traversal operations raise questions about feasibility on severely memory-constrained RISC-V cores lacking the M (multiply) extension. We port all three SPHINCS+-SHA2 and SPHINCS+-SHAKE parameter sets to bare-metal RISC-V RV32I (without M extension) on a 32 kB RAM, 256 kB flash target and measure peak stack depth, heap allocation, code size, and cycle counts. Without a multiplier, SHA-256 compression function throughput drops by 6.1x compared to RV32IM. data.message:
Review the claims of profile R0233.
It is about: researcher Valentina Stojanović (R0233).

Claims:
1. Model-based test generation from contract-based specifications of interrupt-driven firmware using ISR annotations. [SYN-PUB-02947]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-02947] publication · Contract-Based Specification of Interrupt-Driven Firmware for Model-Based Test Generation · 2016 · researchers R0233
Contract-Based Specification of Interrupt-Driven Firmware for Model-Based Test Generation (2016, conference, Proceedings of the International Conference on Formal Techniques for Embedded Systems (FTES)).
Authors: Valentina Stojanović (R0233); Anita Kovačević (outside co-author); Marco Ferreira (outside co-author).
Keywords: contract-based specification; interrupt-driven firmware; ISR testing; model-based test generation; ARM Cortex-M.
Interrupt-driven firmware presents challenges for model-based testing because interleaving of interrupt service routines (ISRs) with the main execution thread produces combinatorial state spaces. This paper proposes a contract language, IFContract, that allows engineers to annotate ISR entry and exit conditions, shared-variable invariants, and timing constraints using a syntax embedded in C comments. A parser translates annotations into an extended FSM representation. Test cases covering pairwise ISR–main-thread interactions are generated from this model. The approach was evaluated on firmware for a battery management unit implemented on an ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller. The generated suite comprised 147 test cases and detected all 38 manually seeded interface faults. Compared with a randomly generated suite of the same size, the model-based suite found 23% more faults. Annotation effort was measured at 2.3 lines of contract per 10 lines of ISR code on average.

[SYN-PUB-05925] publication · Cache-Timing Attacks on ML-KEM (FIPS 203) in a Shared-Memory Embedded RTOS Environment · 2025 · researchers R0503
Cache-Timing Attacks on ML-KEM (FIPS 203) in a Shared-Memory Embedded RTOS Environment (2025, conference, Proceedings of the International Symposium on Secure Computing Systems (ISCS)).
Authors: Miroslav Tešić (outside co-author); Karolina Wójcik (outside co-author); Milica Nikolić (R0503).
Keywords: ML-KEM; cache-timing; FreeRTOS; side-channel; Cortex-M7.
Embedded real-time operating systems increasingly run multiple isolated tasks sharing a common data cache, creating conditions for cache-timing side channels even on microcontrollers. We study ML-KEM (FIPS 203, formerly Kyber) running as a FreeRTOS task on an STM32H743 Cortex-M7 with a 16 kB 4-way set-associative L1 data cache and a co-resident adversarial task with unprivileged access. Using a Prime+Probe variant adapted for the Cortex-M7 cache geometry, the adversary task collects 250,000 cache access measurements and applies a correlation distinguisher to the modular reduction tables. We recover 4 bits of the decapsulation secret with probability greater than 0.8, demonstrating a practical (though partial) leakage channel. We then evaluate three mitigations: cache-line aligned constant-time modular arithmetic, OS-level cache flushing between task switches, and disabling the data cache entirely. The last option increases ML-KEM decapsulation time from 0.31 ms to 1.87 ms and is impractical …[+6597 chars]

Latency Characterisation of Open-Source Real-Time Kernels for Automotive HIL Applications (2016, journal, Real-Time Systems: Theory and Applications).
Authors: Darko Ninkov (R0356); Zoran Marković (outside co-author); Spasoje Petrović (R0868).
Keywords: RTAI; Xenomai; PREEMPT_RT; latency; real-time Linux; HiL benchmarking.
Several open-source options exist for turning a general-purpose Linux system into a deterministic real-time platform: RTAI, Xenomai 3, and the PREEMPT_RT patch. This paper provides a systematic comparison of all three on two hardware platforms—a standard Intel Core i5 desktop and an ARM Cortex-A9 single-board computer—under automotive HiL workloads. Latency was measured using a hardware timer circuit with 100 ns resolution over 72-hour test windows while simultaneously running a 23-state vehicle dynamics model, a CAN stack, and a UDP telemetry stream. Xenomai 3 with the Cobalt core achieved the lowest worst-case latency on the x86 platform at 18 µs, while PREEMPT_RT showed marginally better throughput at the cost of 47 µs worst-case. On the ARM platform, Xenomai 3 and PREEMPT_RT performed comparably. The paper provides configuration recipes, kernel version numbers, and patch sets used, making the results reproducible. Recommendations are given for selecting a kernel flavour based on step-size and I/O bandwidth requirements.

A Regression Testing Strategy for Android Applications Targeting Multiple API Levels Simultaneously (2019, journal, Software Testing International).
Authors: Branislava Dragišić (R0312); Katarina Varga (outside co-author); Radovan Radulović (R0694); Péter Molnár (outside co-author); Jovanka Pejović (outside co-author).
Keywords: regression testing; Espresso; multi-API testing; test tagging; Android.
Maintaining regression test suites that remain valid across a wide span of Android API levels is a practical challenge for small development teams. This paper proposes a layered test architecture in which test cases are tagged with applicability metadata specifying minimum and maximum API levels, deprecation-aware skip conditions, and device-class constraints such as screen density and form factor. The architecture was implemented as an extension to the Espresso UI testing framework and evaluated through a longitudinal case study with three mobile application projects maintained by student teams over two academic semesters. The extended framework reduced the number of false-positive test failures caused by platform differences by 47% compared to unmodified Espresso suites run across the same device pool. The approach added an average overhead of 9% to test execution time. Interviewed developers reported reduced confusion when interpreting test results on mixed-API-level device farms.

[SYN-PUB-03144] publication · A Lightweight ISOBUS Task Controller Client Stack for Microcontrollers with 64 kB Flash · 2022 · researchers R0248
A Lightweight ISOBUS Task Controller Client Stack for Microcontrollers with 64 kB Flash (2022, journal, Microprocessors and Microsystems — Embedded Hardware Design).
Authors: Nemanja Perić (outside co-author); Ivana Bogdanović (outside co-author); Darko Zarić (R0248).
Keywords: TC client; ISOBUS; Cortex-M0+; flash-constrained; DDOP; section control.
Most open-source ISOBUS TC client implementations target MCUs with at least 256 kB of flash, which excludes a large class of low-cost sensor ECUs used on small farm implements in developing or budget-constrained markets. This paper describes the design and verification of a TC-BAS client stack written in C99 that compiles to 47.2 kB on a Cortex-M0+ target at -Os optimisation, leaving adequate space for application code. Design decisions including static DDOP allocation, integer-only arithmetic for device-descriptor encoding, and a two-state process-data pump are detailed. The stack was integrated into a prototype section-control module for a 6 m boom sprayer and tested against four commercial task controllers using the AEF plugfest procedure. Interoperability was confirmed with all four controllers for TC-BAS functionality; two edge cases in setpoint handling were identified …[+2744 chars]

Our quality assurance team writes regression tests by hand for every firmware release; with four hardware variants and monthly release cycles that's eating about 35% of total engineering time and we're still shipping bugs that automated tests should catch.

We release firmware roughly once a month across four hardware variants: the original NetGuard-OT board, the Mini, and two older boards we still maintain for clients under long-term support contracts. Before each release our QA team runs a regression suite that they have been building by hand since 2015. The suite now has around 1,400 test cases. Writing new cases for a feature, updating old ones when hardware behaviour changes, and running everything on four boards takes about two and a half weeks of engineering time per cycle. That is the 35% figure. We have also shipped three bugs in the past year that the regression suite should have caught but did not because the relevant test cases were out of date. Applying Hidden Markov Models to Detect Shifts in Student Learning States from Clickstream Data (2017, journal, Journal of Learning Analytics Research).
Authors: Danilo Mitrović (R1006); Nataša Popović (outside co-author); Christoph Baumann (outside co-author).
Keywords: hidden Markov model; learning states; clickstream; Baum-Welch; engagement dynamics.
Hidden Markov models (HMMs) were fitted to weekly clickstream summaries of 620 students enrolled in a statistics course over one academic year, with the aim of identifying latent learning states and their transition dynamics. Observations consisted of five aggregated behavioural features per week: resource views, forum posts, quiz attempts, assignment submissions, and session duration. A three-state HMM, selected by BIC, was estimated using the Baum–Welch algorithm. The inferred states corresponded interpretably to disengaged, routine, and intensive study behaviours. Transition matrices indicated that recovery from the disengaged state became increasingly improbable after week seven. Keywords: Merkle tree; firmware patch; ECDSA; integrity verification; Cortex-M.
Applying binary patches to firmware in the field requires verification mechanisms that can detect partial or corrupted patch delivery without storing the complete expected image. This paper proposes a Merkle hash tree construction adapted for delta patches, where leaf nodes correspond to fixed-size patch chunks and the root hash is authenticated by an ECDSA signature over NIST P-256. The scheme was implemented on an STM32L4 series microcontroller with 64 KB RAM. Hash tree construction over a 16 KB patch (32 leaves) required 210 ms and consumed a peak of 4.1 KB stack space. Verification of a partial delivery — detecting one corrupted chunk among 32 — required fewer than 50 ms. Review the claims of profile R0503.
It is about: researcher Milica Nikolić (R0503).

Claims:
1. Migration roadmap development targeting IEC 62443 compliance for post-quantum cryptography deployment in critical infrastructure. [SYN-PRJ-0502]

Sources:
[SYN-PRJ-0502] project · Post-Quantum Cryptography for Hardware Security Modules in Critical Infrastructure · 2021 · researchers R0503
PQHSM: Post-Quantum Cryptography for Hardware Security Modules in Critical Infrastructure (Science Fund of the Republic of Serbia (PROMIS, IDEAS, Prizma), 2021–2024).
Participants: R0503 principal investigator.
Partners: RT-RK Institute for Computer Based Systems, Novi Sad; Faculty of Electrical Engineering, University of East Sarajevo; Informatika d.o.o., Novi Sad.
The project investigates the performance and security constraints of deploying post-quantum cryptographic algorithms on hardware security modules used in Serbian energy and transport infrastructure. Work packages cover algorithm selection and adaptation, FPGA and secure microcontroller implementation, side-channel and fault-injection evaluation, and a migration roadmap document targeting IEC 62443 compliance. The team collaborates with the RT-RK Institute in Novi Sad for industrial system integration testing. Outputs include an open benchmarking dataset, two software libraries released under an open-source licence, and a technical report delivered to the Serbian Ministry of Information and Telecommunications.

Review the claims of profile R0248.
It is about: researcher Darko Zarić (R0248).

Claims:
1. Comparative evaluation of ISOBUS conformance test frameworks for task-controller functionality and development of supplementary test script libraries. [SYN-PUB-03140]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-03140] publication · Comparative Evaluation of ISOBUS Conformance Test Suites for Aftermarket Task Controllers · 2016 · researchers R0248
Comparative Evaluation of ISOBUS Conformance Test Suites for Aftermarket Task Controllers (2016, journal, Computers and Electronics in Agriculture Systems).
Authors: Darko Zarić (R0248); Tibor Kovač (outside co-author).
Keywords: ISOBUS conformance; task controller; AEF; test coverage; TC-GEO.
ISO 11783 conformance testing is carried out by accredited laboratories using proprietary test suites, but aftermarket ECU developers frequently rely on open-source or self-developed tools whose coverage is incomplete. This paper documents a structured comparison of three freely available ISOBUS test frameworks against the official AEF conformance test specification version 3.2, focusing on the task controller (TC-BAS, TC-SC, TC-GEO) server functionality. Each framework was applied to the same firmware image running on a prototype TC ECU, and discrepancies in test outcomes were logged across 247 individual test cases. The open-source tools missed 31 to 59 failure conditions identified by the reference suite, primarily in section 9 multi-section control and DDOP version negotiation. The analysis highlights specific gaps and proposes a supplementary test script library written in Python and distributed under an MIT licence that closes 24 of the identified gaps.

[SYN-PUB-07522] publication · Comparison of Frequency-Domain Decomposition and Stochastic Subspace Identification for Damage Localization in Multi-Bay Steel Frames · 2015 · researchers R0666
Comparison of Frequency-Domain Decomposition and Stochastic Subspace Identification for Damage Localization in Multi-Bay Steel Frames (2015, journal, Journal of Vibration Diagnostics and Structural Integrity).
Authors: Jelena Jokić (R0666); Dragan Milošević (outside co-author); Attila Varga (outside co-author).
Keywords: FDD; SSI-COV; damage index; multi-bay frame; damage localization.
Two widely used OMA algorithms—frequency-domain decomposition (FDD) and stochastic subspace identification (SSI-COV)—are compared for their ability to localize damage in a three-bay, two-storey welded steel frame model. Damage was simulated by progressively cutting a weld in the lower right column-beam connection in three stages, reducing net throat area by 20%, 40%, and 60%. Ambient excitation was provided by pedestrian-like loading applied at the floor levels. Both algorithms identified natural frequencies within 0.15 Hz of each other for the first six modes. Damage localization was assessed via the modal strain energy damage index (MSEDI). SSI-COV achieved correct panel identification at 20% damage in 7 of 10 repeated trials, while FDD achieved correct localization in only 4 of 10 at the same damage level. At 40% and 60% damage, both methods localized correctly in all trials. The study recommends SSI-COV for early-stage damage detection when signal-to-noise conditions are moderate.

Fractographic Classification of Stress Corrosion Fracture Modes in Quenched-and-Tempered Bolt Steels: A Comparative SEM Study (2026, journal, Materials Characterisation and Testing).
Authors: Miloš Ivanović (R0719); Dragana Vučković (outside co-author); Zoran Mitrović (outside co-author).
Keywords: fractography; SEM; quenched-and-tempered steel; intergranular cracking; SCC fracture modes.
Fracture surface morphologies arising from stress corrosion cracking in three quenched-and-tempered steels used in structural fastener production (42CrMo4, 34CrNiMo6, and 30CrNiMo8) were systematically characterised by scanning electron microscopy following slow strain rate tests in acidic chloride solution (pH 3.5, 0.1 M NaCl, 1×10⁻⁶ s⁻¹). Each steel was tested at two tempering temperatures (450 °C and 550 °C) to produce ultimate tensile strengths ranging from approximately 1050 MPa to 1350 MPa. A total of 36 fracture surfaces were imaged and classified according to the proportion of intergranular, transgranular quasi-cleavage, and ductile dimple areas using image analysis software. The 34CrNiMo6 steel at the higher strength level showed the largest intergranular fraction (41%), while 42CrMo4 tempered at 550 °C exhibited the lowest susceptibility index and predominantly ductile fracture. Crack initiation sites were associated with inclusions and prior austenite grain boundary triple junctions. The claim combines MC/DC (from SYN-PUB-04578, which is about embedded C) with the PLC ST data-flow criteria (from SYN-PUB-04587) as a single unified topic 'for safety-critical software including … all adapted to PLC Structured Text', but SYN-PUB-04578 does not cover PLC ST and SYN-PUB-04583 does not cover any of the listed coverage criteria for PLC ST.

claim.text: Counterexample generation and minimisation techniques in software model checking, with focus on concurrent and interrupt-driven embedded programs.

rejected.reason: SYN-PUB-04581 surveys counterexample generation techniques in software model checking and identifies a gap regarding concurrent embedded programs; SYN-PUB-04582 covers CBMC-based verification of interrupt-driven embedded programs; however, neither source covers 'counterexample minimisation techniques' — SYN-PUB-04581 identifies minimisation as a gap in the literature rather than a contribution, and SYN-PUB-04582 does not address minimisation. SYN-PUB-04579 is cited but is about bounded model checking of timed automata, not counterexample minimisation.

claim.text: Incremental verification of firmware patches using change-impact analysis and reuse of SMT satisfiability certificates to reduce verification cost.

rejected.reason: SYN-PUB-04586 presents incremental verification of patched firmware using change-impact analysis and reuse of SMT unsatisfiability certificates (referred to in the claim as 'satisfiability certificates', whereas the paper specifically uses 'unsatisfiability certificates'), which is a factual distinction; however, the core method and all other facts are supported. The claim says 'SMT satisfiability certificates' but the source states 'SMT unsatisfiability certificates', which is a different technical term and a fact the claim changes.

Review the claims of pair C003-CH2:R0995.
It is about: researcher Veljko Pantelić (R0995) and company AutomVoj a.d. (C003), challenge C003-CH2.

Claims:
1. AutomVoj must push safety patches across 38 separate PLC codebases in TIA Portal and cannot afford a full rewrite while engineers are on active commissioning projects. [C003-CH2]
2. Pantelić co-authored a paper on extraction and recovery of implicit variability from legacy PLC codebases using clone detection and feature model synthesis. [SYN-PUB-10379]
3. Pantelić co-authored a paper on incremental generation strategies for PLC software that reduce regeneration time while preserving manually authored customisation sections. [SYN-PUB-02958]
4. Pantelić led SAFEPLL, an Interreg IPA project integrating functional safety requirements into PLC product-line workflows, producing methodology documents adopted by two SME automation integrators as internal guidelines. [SYN-PRJ-0391]
5. Pantelić led PLCGEN, a Science Fund project that delivered an Eclipse-based IDE plugin and transformation library for model-driven PLC product-line engineering, with validation on industrial automation projects. [SYN-PRJ-0390]
6. Pantelić and AutomVoj would apply variability recovery and incremental model-driven generation methods to the 38 TIA Portal PLC codebases (C003-CH2), using clone detection and feature model synthesis to identify shared and variable logic (SYN-PUB-10379), then produce a modular IEC 61131-3 product-line library with incremental generation strategies that preserve manually authored sections (SYN-PUB-02958), so that future safety patches can be propagated from a single model rather than applied to each codebase individually. [C003-CH2, SYN-PUB-10379, SYN-PUB-02958]
7. The published variability-recovery work covers IEC 61131-3 Structured Text; AutomVoj's 38 codebases are written in ladder logic in TIA Portal, and the records do not confirm the method has been applied to ladder logic or TIA Portal specifically. [SYN-PUB-1…[+10213 chars]

SAFEPLL: Safety-Aware Product-Line Modelling for Certified Automation Software (Interreg IPA Hungary–Serbia, 2022–2024).
Participants: R0995 work package leader; R0749 team member.
Partners: Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad; Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Hungary; Automatika-Pro d.o.o., Novi Sad; RoboSystems Kft., Pécs, Hungary.
SAFEPLL addressed the integration of functional safety requirements into model-driven PLC product-line workflows, targeting IEC 62061 SIL 1 and SIL 2 certified applications. The project brought together researchers from Novi Sad and Budapest with two SME automation integrators. Veljko Pantelić led the work package on traceability from HAZOP artefacts to generated code, contributing the SysML parametric diagram transformation described in the 2021 conference paper. The project produced a methodology document adopted by both industrial partners as an internal development guideline, and delivered training workshops for engineering staff at both companies.

Review the claims of pair C003-CH2:R0995.
It is about: researcher Veljko Pantelić (R0995) and company AutomVoj a.d. (C003), challenge C003-CH2.

Claims:
1. Pantelić led the traceability work package in SAFEPLL, an Interreg IPA project integrating functional safety requirements into PLC product-line workflows; the project produced a methodology document adopted by both SME automation integrators as an internal development guideline. [SYN-PRJ-0391]

Sources:
[SYN-PRJ-0391] project · Safety-Aware Product-Line Modelling for Certified Automation Software · 2022 · researchers R0995, R0749
SAFEPLL: Safety-Aware Product-Line Modelling for Certified Automation Software (Interreg IPA Hungary–Serbia, 2022–2024).
Participants: R0995 work package leader; R0749 team member.
Partners: Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad; Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Hungary; Automatika-Pro d.o.o., Novi Sad; RoboSystems Kft., Pécs, Hungary.
SAFEPLL addressed the integration of functional safety requirements into model-driven PLC product-line workflows, targeting IEC 62061 SIL 1 and SIL 2 certified applications. The project brought together researchers from Novi Sad and Budapest with two SME automation integrators. Veljko Pantelić led the work package on traceability from HAZOP artefacts to generated code, contributing the SysML parametric diagram transformation described in the 2021 conference paper. The project produced a methodology document adopted by both industrial partners as an internal development guideline, and delivered training workshops for engineering staff at both companies.

Review the claims of profile R0375.
It is about: researcher Stefan Kostić (R0375).

Claims:
1. Counterexample generation techniques in software model checking, including CEGAR-based refinement, interpolant-based approaches, and SMT-guided path enumeration. [SYN-PUB-04581]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-04581] publication · A Survey of Counterexample Generation Techniques in Software Model Checking · 2018 · researchers R0375
A Survey of Counterexample Generation Techniques in Software Model Checking (2018, book chapter, Advances in Formal Methods for Embedded and Cyber-Physical Systems, Springer).
Authors: Rok Štruc (outside co-author); Stefan Kostić (R0375); Andreja Kovačič (outside co-author).
Keywords: counterexample generation; CEGAR; software model checking; survey; concurrent programs.
This chapter reviews counterexample generation methods used in software model checking tools from 2005 to 2017, covering CEGAR-based refinement, interpolant-based approaches, and SMT-guided path enumeration. The survey organises 62 primary studies along four dimensions: the underlying logic fragment used, the class of properties addressed, scalability with respect to program size, and quality of counterexample explanation for human reviewers. We identify a gap in the literature regarding counterexample minimisation for concurrent embedded programs: only 7 of the 62 studies address concurrency, and fewer than half provide mechanically reproducible experimental setups. The chapter concludes with a discussion of open problems, including the need for domain-specific explanation formats suited to control engineers who are not formal methods specialists, and the relationship between counterexample quality and debugging time in industrial settings.

EMC Filter Design for SiC MOSFET-Based Motor Drives: Comparison with IGBT Baseline at 150 kHz–30 MHz (2021, conference, Proceedings of the 22nd European Conference on Power Electronics and Applications (EPE-ECCE Europe)).
Authors: Ana Mamužić (R0283); Nikola Đorđević (outside co-author); Thomas Berger (outside co-author).
Keywords: SiC MOSFET; IGBT comparison; rise time; high-frequency EMI; four-stage filter.
Silicon carbide MOSFET inverters switch at voltages and currents with rise times below 50 ns, generating significantly higher high-frequency conducted emissions than conventional IGBT-based drives of equivalent power rating. This work compares the conducted emission spectra of a 7.5 kW SiC MOSFET drive (switching at 50 kHz) and an IGBT baseline (switching at 8 kHz) under the same load, and documents the additional filter attenuation required to achieve IEC 61800-3 Category C2 compliance for the SiC case. The SiC drive exceeded the Category C2 quasi-peak limit by up to 22 dB in the 5–30 MHz band compared to 9 dB for the IGBT. An optimised four-stage LC filter reduced the worst-case exceedance to within the 6 dB safety margin, at the cost of a 40% increase in filter volume relative to the IGBT design. Measured and simulated spectra agree within ±3 dB across the full range.

HARMIND: Harmonic Mitigation Strategies for Multi-Level Inverter-Fed Industrial Drives in Medium-Voltage Distribution Networks (Science Fund of the Republic of Serbia (PROMIS, IDEAS, Prizma), 2021–2024).
Participants: R0567 principal investigator.
Partners: Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, Serbia; Faculty of Electronic Engineering, University of Niš, Serbia; Agroind Vojvodina d.o.o., Zrenjanin, Serbia.
The project investigated harmonic emission and mitigation strategies for cascaded H-bridge and neutral-point-clamped inverter drives connected to 6 kV and 10 kV industrial distribution networks. Work packages covered reformulated SHE-PWM methods, passive and hybrid active filter design, network-level harmonic interaction modelling in PSCAD, and a measurement campaign at two industrial sites in Vojvodina. The project involved collaboration with the Faculty of Electronic Engineering in Niš and a local industrial partner from the food processing sector. Results included improved SHE-PWM formulations tolerant to DC-link imbalance, validated filter design procedures, and a publicly available measurement dataset from the industrial sites.

Interference between ripple control signals and supraharmonic emissions in distribution networks: a time-domain case study (2018, journal, International Journal of Electrical Power and Energy Systems).
Authors: Stefan Horvat (outside co-author); Gábor Fekete (outside co-author); Nataša Vuković (outside co-author); Danijela Ninkov (R0611).

We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.

Our ProtoSense module watches Modbus and BACnet traffic and is supposed to flag anything that looks wrong. The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. A few of them have been running their networks for twenty years with no security monitoring at all, so if they were compromised they would not know.
